title: Beginner To Master | Chess Speedrun | 1440 | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: f3 is the Sämisch — it props up a future e4. In true King's Indian spirit we don't fight it; we just fianchetto and let White build the centre.
moves.teaches: Against the Sämisch, don't contest e4 directly — fianchetto and prepare to strike the centre later.

moves.spoken: d6 stops e5, and then we castle and finish development.
Bd3 is an instructive inaccuracy — and it goes to the heart of why the King's Indian is so annoying: White carelessly severs the queen from the d4-pawn, leaving it weak.
moves.teaches: Watch for the moment White's own move disconnects the defense of his centre pawn — that's your target.

moves.spoken: Normally we'd hit d4 with a pawn, but c5 or e5 here just lets White push d5. So Nc6 is the move — attack the pawn with a piece instead.
moves.teaches: When a pawn break lets the opponent lock the centre, pressure the target with a piece rather than a pawn.

moves.spoken: Nd7 is the subtle reroute — it brings the g7-bishop to life, and remember, bad bishops defend good pawns. Now e5 comes with real force.
moves.teaches: Reroute a knight to unblock your fianchetto bishop before you strike in the centre.

moves.spoken: Now e5 strikes at d4, and if White pushes d5, the central square opens for our pieces.
Nd4 is the payoff — the bishop supports the square and the knight plants itself on the finest central outpost.
moves.teaches: Occupy the outpost your bishop already supports; it can never be dislodged by a pawn.

moves.spoken: The knight tour continues to c5 — look at the pressure these two knights pour onto White's position.
When the knight is attacked by a third piece, don't defend it — let White spend time capturing it while we coordinate and strike. f5 fires up the attack.
moves.teaches: Rather than passively defend an attacked piece, let it go for tempo and open your own attack.

moves.spoken: Bh6 is a blunder — a type-two piece, defended only once. Combine that with the diagonal f3 weakened: once the f6-knight steps aside, the queen swings to h4, and the bishop falls with the game.
moves.teaches: After f3, remember the queen's route to h4; unmask it by moving the f6-knight to snap off a loose piece.

moves.spoken: Use the method of comparison — a pawn on e7 instead of e5 means you can chip at the d5-pawn with e6 and c6, ripping the centre open to punish the weaknesses f3 created.
moves.teaches: Open the centre against a Sämisch to expose the very holes the early f3 left behind.
